analysis.one_liner: Extends the tariff on imported ethanol through 2015.
analysis.headline: A four-member bill to extend the tariff on imported ethanol through 2015 never got a vote; it died in the Ways and Means Committee when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have extended an import tax on ethanol, previously scheduled to expire January 1, 2012, for three more years, through January 1, 2015. The tariff (historically about 54 cents per gallon on top of a small percentage duty) makes ethanol from abroad, mainly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol, more expensive than domestic corn ethanol. The bill was introduced by Rep. Charles Rangel with three cosponsors in December 2011 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic corn ethanol producers and, through them, corn growers, who would keep cheaper foreign ethanol shut out of the market for three more years and could sell more of their product to gasoline blenders at higher prices.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Harmonized Tariff Schedule to extend the additional duty on ethanol through January 1, 2015, instead of its scheduled January 1, 2012 expiration. [S2][S3]
The higher tariff would keep ethanol imports, chiefly Brazilian sugarcane ethanol, more expensive than domestic corn ethanol, protecting the market share and prices of U.S. ethanol producers.

analysis.who_pays: Gasoline blenders and fuel consumers, who would pay more for ethanol because cheaper imported ethanol would carry the tariff; foreign ethanol producers, mainly Brazilian, would lose U.S. sales.

drawbacks.text: The tariff raises the cost of ethanol used in gasoline, a cost that blenders pass on at the pump, in order to shield domestic producers from cheaper imports. [S3]

By the time the bill was introduced, Congress had already let the ethanol blender's tax credit expire at the end of 2011, so this bill would have kept a mature, heavily subsidized industry protected from competition without the offsetting consumer credit (widely reported).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go narrowly to ethanol producers and corn growers; its costs are spread across everyone who buys gasoline, in the form of higher ethanol prices. Extending a protective tariff for three years for a small sponsor group's industry, with no hearing or public debate, weighs against it; the offset is that it never became law.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 2, 2011, referred to the Ways and Means Committee, then to its Trade Subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Rangel introduced the bill on December 2, 2011, joined by Reps. Burton of Indiana, Payne, and Engel. [S3]
The House referred it to the Committee on Ways and Means on December 2, 2011. [S5]
On December 7, 2011, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Trade, where the record ends. [S5]
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013. [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and gasoline blenders are better off, because the ethanol import tariff expired on schedule at the end of 2011 and this bill did not revive it; Brazilian ethanol producers likewise kept their access to the U.S. market.

for.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the ethanol tariff.

for.name: Reps. Dan Burton, Donald Payne, and Eliot Engel

against.name: Rep. Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before his committee; after referral, the only action was a second referral to the Trade Subcommittee, with no markup or vote. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and two cosponsors were Democrats and one cosponsor was a Republican; no vote ever occurred, so party lines were never tested.

industries.note: The tariff would have kept cheaper Brazilian sugarcane ethanol out of the U.S. market for three more years, letting domestic producers sell more at higher prices. The cost shows up in the price of ethanol blended into gasoline.
Higher domestic ethanol demand supports corn prices, but the benefit comes from a tariff that raises fuel costs for consumers.
The tariff makes their product more expensive in the U.S. market and costs them sales; their interest here runs with consumers who want cheaper fuel inputs.
Blenders pay the duty on imported ethanol and pass the cost into gasoline prices; they had just lost the blender's tax credit at the end of 2011, and this bill offered no replacement.
